featured.question: How do you assess promising model architectures whose researchers leave scaling to someone else?
featured.answer: There are a lot of interesting proposed architectures that I come across where the researcher is leaving scaling to someone else because they don't have the resources, but it still leaves a big question as to whether you'll see the expected results at scale. I think for folks who are experienced in scaling and have had the fortune of being one, it's truly an art and a science to get it right. It's not just like we change this thing and we change this other thing and it just works. It's a fun adventure every single time.

featured.question: How do you judge whether a jailbreak is universal within the domain of cybersecurity?
featured.answer: An example: an adversary cyber attacker needs it to not just help find vulnerabilities, but also develop exploits for them, actually leverage those exploits to compromise computer systems. We wouldn't consider it to be universal if it helped you find bugs in code, but didn't help you with these kinds of more operational parts of an attack. But if it worked across all of cybersecurity, but didn't for something like making anthrax, we'd still consider that universal in the domain of cyber.

featured.question: How do you categorize enterprise generative AI use cases that you see as having product-market fit today?
featured.answer: It's really hard to categorize. I think there's some vertical applications. For example, in healthcare, we really want to make note-taking and form-filling much easier for doctors. Having passive listening mics and being able to listen to that doctor-patient interaction and pre-populate things so that they're not spending half their time typing notes and that type of thing. I think that's very vertical-specific, but much more of what we see are these general categories. Customer support is something where the technology is ready and the need is very much there, and so that's moving quite quickly across verticals—in telco, in healthcare, in financial services. Everybody needs this capability, and the technology is there for it.

featured.question: Why do you think real-time agents might need a better notion of interruptible work?
featured.answer: As I think about how this needs to change, there might need to be some better notion of interruptible work for agents on their side. As a thing is off working, if you try to ping it, it just won't respond. You don't even know what it's doing, which is really frustrating. featured.question: What do you think of Karl Friston’s theory of learning as minimizing surprise?
featured.answer: I think it's very underspecified. There's this category of theories in science of things that have a good combination of intuitively being in the right direction and then have a lot of math, but it's actually very hard to connect them to experiments and to an empirical research program. I think there's something right about the fact that children and people in general, when they're learning, are looking for violations of their predictions and something like surprise. But I'm a little skeptical about whether that formalism isn't going to end up accounting for everything. I think it's one of those kinds of theories. It's certainly very closely related to ideas that come out of the theory theory framework, which include things like, what you should be doing is making predictions, and you should be exploring things that are surprising and don't fit the predictions that you already have.

featured.question: How do you understand the role of military-economic competition in making technological adoption inevitable?
featured.answer: One famous quote in the history of technology that was arguing against determinism was that technology doesn’t force us to do anything; it merely opens the door. It makes possible new ways of living, new forms of life. And my retort was: technology doesn’t force us; it merely opens the door—and it’s military economic competition that forces us through. So when a new technology comes on the stage, many groups can choose to ignore it or do whatever they will with it. But if one group chooses to employ it in this functional way that gives them some advantage, eventually the pressure from that group will come to all the rest and either force them to adopt or lead the other group to losing their resources to the new, more fit group.

featured.question: Why do you see neural operators as a way to overcome the limitations of physics-informed neural networks?
featured.answer: PINNs don't work everywhere, and our idea of neural operators came as a way to overcome this. We can't rely just on physics constraints alone to come up with answers. We have lots of data available. I'll talk about the weather example, where we even collect data. We don't just solve equations and have synthetic data, but we also have real data by observing the weather. Why not make use of all of the data available? We don't just rely on trying to solve partial differential equations and other physical problems from scratch, because it's really the data driven approach that makes it possible to get quick answers. featured.question: How do you understand Anthropic’s J-space paper as evidence of reasoning inside AI models?

We can apply it to a model to tell us, in the model's latent activation space—because everything is essentially vectors—which directions will cause the model to say certain particular words later. We've also done this in the output distribution. If that is small, we exit. The idea is that the model's converging on some thought or idea.

featured.question: How do you understand the role of math in training reasoning models?

It's one of the core types of science. But also in many ways, it's just happened by coincidence to be a thing that we focused on. But it's not necessarily the end product of what we even want to focus on in research. We're now realizing, OK, if we can do this for math, can we scale this up for other types of science, for professional work, for capabilities that are useful to humans on a personal level? about: People: for each guest in a corpus of 355 AI podcast episodes, reviewers went through their episodes from newest to oldest and kept the first substantive long-form interview. For guests with fewer than 20 questions, older episodes were added until they passed 20 or ran out.
Transcripts: gpt-6-luna (medium) cleaned each transcript turn by turn, keeping the speakers' own words, removing filler and backchannels, merging continuations and repairing caption speaker labels.

Questions: for every guest answer of 30 or more words, gpt-6.1-sol (medium) wrote interview-style questions about how the guest understands an entity or event, keeping only those whose answer shows judgment or taste. Each answer is the guest's own reply in the first person, supported by verbatim quotes from the cleaned transcript.
Rubrics: gpt-6.1-sol (medium) turned each answer into one-idea criteria with the v10 rubric writer. Rubrics are what a model's answer is checked against.

Model results: Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1, Astra 6 and Sol 6.1 answered every question as the guest at low reasoning effort, seeing only a one-line host introduction and the question, with no tools. gpt-6-luna (high effort) judged each answer against the rubrics without seeing the guest's answer. Scores measure coverage of the guest's ideas, not overall answer quality. Questions that any model refused (Anthropic's biology usage filter blocked five, from James Zou and Paul-Enguerrand Fady) are dropped for every model. Karthik Narasimhan, Zhuang Liu and Ray Dalio use questions from the previous version of this note (same question-writing method, ElevenLabs transcripts), answered and judged the same way.
